opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is really computational cost, and how that forces a trade-off with resolution. Traditional climate and weather models are built on numerical solvers for partial differential equations: fluid dynamics, thermodynamics, radiation, and so on. To capture the processes that matter, like cloud formation, convection, and turbulence, you need very fine resolution, sometimes down to a kilometer or less. But the cost of these solvers scales dramatically as you refine the grid. Even on the biggest supercomputers in the world, running at that resolution for long climate time scales is prohibitively expensive.

So what happens in practice is that people run at coarse resolution and then rely on what are called parameterizations. These are approximate, often hand-tuned models of the small-scale physics you can't resolve directly. That's a major source of uncertainty in climate projections. Clouds, for example, are one of the largest uncertainties in estimating climate sensitivity.

The other consequence is that you can only afford a handful of simulations. If you want to understand extreme events, like a once-in-a-hundred-year heat wave or a hurricane intensifying rapidly, you need large ensembles, thousands of runs, to properly characterize the tails of the distribution. With traditional methods, that's just not feasible.

That's where AI comes in, and why we've been working on neural operators. With FourCastNet, for instance, we showed you can get forecasts that are competitive with traditional numerical weather prediction while being tens of thousands of times faster. And because neural operators learn mappings between function spaces rather than at a fixed grid, they can work across resolutions. You can train on a mix of coarse and fine data and still query at high resolution. That opens the door to the huge ensembles and fine-scale detail that traditional modeling has simply been unable to afford.

r001.rationale: The response names computational cost as the biggest bottleneck and says that even running a model at fine resolution over long climate timescales is prohibitively expensive.

r002.rationale: It explicitly connects the cost of refining the grid to the need to run at coarse resolution, limiting high-resolution climate modeling.

fable-5.1.text:
The biggest bottleneck is really computation, and it comes from the physics itself. Traditional climate and weather models are numerical solvers for partial differential equations, the Navier-Stokes equations and so on, and to solve them you discretize the atmosphere into a grid. The finer the grid, the more accurate you are, but the cost explodes. If you want to halve the grid spacing, you don't just double the compute, you're looking at something like an order of magnitude more, because you have to refine in three spatial dimensions and shrink the time step as well.

So in practice, global models run at resolutions of tens of kilometers. That means the phenomena that actually matter for extreme events, things like convection, cloud formation, the fine structure of a hurricane's eyewall, happen below the grid scale. The model can't resolve them, so you have to parameterize them, write approximate rules for what's happening inside each grid cell. Those parameterizations are hand-crafted, they carry a lot of uncertainty, and a large fraction of the disagreement between climate models traces back to them, especially to clouds.

And then there's the time dimension. If you want to characterize risk, you don't want one forecast, you want thousands of ensemble members so you can say something meaningful about the tail, the one-in-a-hundred-year flood or heat wave. With a model that takes hours on a supercomputer for a single run, you simply can't afford that. Operational centers run maybe fifty members. For climate projections it's even worse, because you're running decades or centuries of simulation.

That's really what motivated our work on neural operators and FourCastNet. The idea is that instead of discretizing and stepping through the equations, you learn the solution operator directly, in a way that's resolution-independent, and then inference is tens of thousands of times faster. Once you have that speedup, the entire calculus changes. You can run enormous ensembles, you can do probabilistic forecasting of extremes, you can push toward kilometer scale. The bottleneck isn't that we don't understand the physics, it's that we can't afford to compute it at the scale where it matters, and that's the gap I think machine learning can close.

r001.rationale: It names computation as the biggest bottleneck and says a single model run takes hours on a supercomputer, making extensive runs unaffordable.

r002.rationale: It explains that finer grids sharply increase computational cost, leaving global models at tens-of-kilometers resolution and limiting kilometer-scale predictions.

astra-6.text:
The biggest bottleneck is computation. Climate models have to capture processes across a huge range of scales, from local cloud formation to global atmospheric circulation. Resolving all of that directly is enormously expensive, so you have to make tradeoffs between resolution, how long you simulate, and how many scenarios you can explore.

That also limits our ability to quantify uncertainty. You need many simulations to understand the range of possible outcomes, especially for extreme events. That’s where AI can help: accelerating these simulations while preserving the physics, so we can explore more scenarios at higher resolution.

r001.rationale: The response identifies climate modeling as computationally expensive, but does not say that even a single simulation run is expensive.

r002.rationale: It links the expense of resolving climate processes across scales to tradeoffs in resolution, supporting the criterion that computational expense limits high-resolution predictions.

sol-6.1.text: The biggest bottleneck is computation. Climate models have to capture processes across a huge range of scales, from local cloud formation to global atmospheric circulation. To resolve finer details, you need a finer grid and smaller time steps, and the computational cost grows very quickly. So you’re forced to approximate processes you can’t resolve, and those approximations introduce uncertainty. That also limits how many simulations you can run to explore different scenarios and understand extreme events.

r001.rationale: The response calls computation the biggest bottleneck and says costs grow quickly, but does not identify the expense of even one simulation run.

r002.rationale: It explains that finer resolution requires finer grids and smaller time steps, which sharply increases computational cost and forces unresolved processes to be approximated.
